pages.name: Introduction
pages.subtitle: OVERVIEW
pages.html:
Introduction

Students are now ready to learn the Five Phonetic Skills. These Five Phonetic Skills help students learn likely and unlikely sequences of letters. In the past, students have been asked to sound words phonetically and have applied sight words adequately. Now they must “prove” the word.

Scientifically Based Method

The Reading Horizons method is a scientifically based method. It is explicit, systematic, sequential phonics taught through multi-sensory, direct instruction.

Delivery Method
  • Have the students stand at smart screens, whiteboards, or chalkboards
  • Dictate the letter, sound, or word twice to the students
  • Use your hands to draw attention to your mouth
  • Students repeat twice and write once on the board
  • Students benefit from active engagement
  • The delivery method employs their auditory, visual, tactile, and kinaesthetic modalities

pages.name: Teacher / Parent
pages.subtitle: METHODOLOGY
pages.html:
Teacher / Parent
Oral and Audio-visual Training (Sight and Ear Training)
  • STUDY the letters with their name’s “A” and sounds /a/.
  • SAY the names “A” and the sounds /a/ aloud for the student to be able to recognize the names “a” and the sounds /a/ in the next page.
Note: Research shows that knowing all the alphabet is very important. All students, regardless of age, should review the alphabet. The time spent on the introduction or review depends on the student’s age and ability.

pages.name: Consonant and Vowel Slide
pages.subtitle: INTRODUCTION
pages.html:
Consonant and Vowel Slide

A consonant is added to the beginning of a vowel to form a new sound. A slide arrow is used to show that the two letters slide together. All vowels have the short sound.

ma
Slide Example
The Slide is a very important step in fluency. Begin by saying the sound /m/, and slide to /a/. The sound produced is /ma/.

Introduction to Blends

A Blend is two or three consonants standing together, each letter keeping its own sound. Blends can appear at the beginning or end of a single-syllable word. Blends are difficult to pronounce in isolation — slide to a vowel sound right away. An arc is used to identify a blend in a word.

pages.name: Digraphs
pages.subtitle: INTRODUCTION
pages.html:
Digraphs

Digraphs are made up of consonants and are joined by an arc. They differ from blends in that the letters that make up a blend keep their own sounds, but in digraphs the letters together make only one sound.

CH, SH, WH, TH (voiceless), TH (voiced), TCH

These digraphs make new sounds. You can pronounce them with a vowel element, so they are easy to hear.

Cheat
Marked Example
Ship
Marked Example
Thing
Marked Example
That
Marked Example
Match
Marked Example
Which
Marked Example
More Digraphs: PH, GH, KN, CK, WR

These digraphs are not new sounds, but new spellings for sounds already learned. The PH digraph has /f/. GN and KN share the same sound /n/. WR has the sound of /r/. CK has the sound /k/.

pages.name: Digraph Blends
pages.subtitle: INTRODUCTION
pages.html:
Digraph Blends
  • R can be joined with unvoiced TH
  • When L, R, and S are added to the digraph CH, it causes CH to change from /ch/ to /k/
  • L and R can be added to the Digraph PH
  • L and R are the final consonant in a Digraph Blend, and S is the initial consonant in a Digraph Blend

The Digraph Blends are SHR, THR, CHL, CHR, SCH, PHL, and PHR. When proving words with Digraph Blends, mark all three letters together.

pages.name: Phonetic Skills
pages.subtitle: PROVING OF WORDS
pages.html:
Phonetic Skills

In the past students have been asked only to “read”, but now they must “prove” the pronunciation of the words they read.

There are five (5) phonetic skills that help students learn and prove likely and unlikely sequences of letters.

Phonetic Skill #1

First, go under the word and mark the vowel with an X. A ‘guardian star’ is always placed over the ‘guardian consonant’ that follows a vowel — the job of the guardian star is to make the vowel short. Now the word has been proven.

Net
Marked Example
Slap
Marked Example
If there is one guardian consonant, the vowel is short.

pages.name: Adding Suffixes to Words Following Phonetic Skills 1 and 2
pages.mainTitle: Adding Suffixes to Words Following Phonetic Skills 1 and 2
pages.subtitle: _ING, _ED, _ER, _EST
pages.html:
Adding Suffixes to Words Following Phonetic Skills 1 and 2

To add the suffixes _ing, _ed, _er, and _est to words following Phonetic Skills 1 and 2, there must be one or two guardians. To add suffixes to a word, students first prove the base word.

If a word follows Phonetic Skill 1, students double the final consonant of the base word and then add the suffix. Then students underline the suffix.

Set → Setting → Setter
Marked Example
Top → Topper → Toppest
Marked Example

If a word follows Phonetic Skill 2, students first prove the base word. They just maintain the base word and add the suffix. Then students underline the suffix.

Jump → Jumped → Jumping
Marked Example
Fast → Faster → Fastest
Marked Example

pages.subtitle: _ING, _ED, _ER, _EST

If a word follows Phonetic Skill 4, students first prove the base word. Drop the final or silent “e” and add the suffix. Then students underline the suffix.

pages.name: Rainbow Sounds
pages.subtitle: 1. ANOTHER SOUND FOR C
pages.html:
Rainbow Sounds

When C is followed by a, o, or u, it usually says the “hard sound” /k/. When C is followed by an i or an e, the sound produced is /s/, or the “soft sound” of C. The new marking is called a rainbow s.

Cat
Marked Example
Cite
Marked Example
Cent
Marked Example

The new sound for C also applies when C is followed by a silent e. If the word ends in _CE, the e will be silent, but the C will still make the /s/ sound.

Twice
Marked Example

pages.name: Rainbow Sounds
pages.subtitle: 2. ANOTHER SOUND FOR G
pages.html:
Rainbow Sounds

When G is followed by a, o, or u, it usually says its hard sound /g/. When G is followed by i or e, it frequently has the soft sound /j/. The new marking is called Rainbow j.

Gum
Marked Example
Gem
Marked Example

The new sound for G also applies when G is followed by a silent e. If the word ends in _GE, the e will be silent, but the G will still make the /j/ sound.

pages.name: Many Jobs of Y
pages.subtitle: INTRODUCTION
pages.html:
Many Jobs of Y

The letter Y says its consonant sound only if it is the first letter in a word. If Y comes anywhere else in the word, it will function as a vowel. To determine its vowel sound, apply the Five Phonetic Skills.

In Phonetic Skill 1

If Y is the only vowel and it has one guardian, it will have the short sound of I.

Myth
Marked Example
In Phonetic Skill 2

If Y is the only vowel and it has two guardians, it will have the short sound of I.

Crypt
Marked Example
In Phonetic Skill 3

If Y is the only vowel and is at the end of the word, it will have the sound of long I.

Try
Marked Example
In Phonetic Skill 4

When Y is the only vowel in a word with Silent E, Y will have the sound of long I.

Type
Marked Example

pages.subtitle: PHONETIC SKILL 5
pages.html:
Many Jobs of Y
In Phonetic Skill 5

When Y is an adjacent vowel, it is silent.
